Among the lush flower-fi elds of Valedayn, slow plodding bloomux graze in great herds. Sipping nectar from the leagues of flowering 
fi elds with their long prehensile proboscises, these peaceful arthropods, standing at nearly seven feet tall, want nothing more than 
to grow their honeywombs for their gestating pupae during the summer. When predators approach the herd, the nectarivores will 
turn their spiny backsides outwards to dissuade any foolish hunter that attempts to get near. Th ough this presents their precious 
honeywombs to the attacker, the potential explosion of chitinous spikes, sticky nectar and wriggling pupae often proves fatal to 
predators, and allows the larvae to be eaten by scavengers for the next stage in their development.

Encountering Th ese ponderous beasts are easy to spot in large 
swarms of twenty to sixty individuals, roaming south to north as 
the fi elds bloom. While they are not a species liable to stampede, 
if the swarm feels endangered they’ll be quick to turn their spines 
outward to ward off any dangerous predators, only sacrifi cing 
themselves in a sequence of fatal eruptions in the most direst of 
situations to save their young pupae.
